issues.legal_issue: A second appeal must be heard and decided only on substantial questions of law formulated by the High Court, unless it formulates an additional substantial question after recording reasons.
material_facts: The High Court formulated two questions of law when admitting the second appeal.
It did not decide either formulated question and did not formulate any additional substantial question with reasons.
Instead, it reappreciated the evidence and reversed the findings of the courts below.
The Supreme Court concluded that the formulated questions were not substantial questions of law arising from the findings of the courts below.
issues.conclusion: The High Court exceeded its jurisdiction by deciding the second appeal through reappreciation of evidence without deciding a substantial question of law properly involved in the case. Its judgment was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the existence of a substantial question of law is a condition for exercising second-appellate jurisdiction, and the appeal must be heard on the question formulated. The High Court may hear an additional substantial question only if satisfied that the case involves it and records reasons for that satisfaction. Under Santosh Hazari v. Purushottam Tiwari, a substantial question must be debatable, unsettled by law or binding precedent, materially affect the parties’ rights, have a foundation in the pleadings, emerge from sustainable factual findings, and be necessary to decide the case. These principles are also supported by Kshitish Chandra Purkait v. Santosh Kumar Purkait, Panchugopal Barua v. Umesh Chandra Goswami, Kondiba Dagadu Kadam v. Savitribai Sopan Gujar, and Thiagarajan v. Sri Venugopalaswamay B. Koil.

predicates.second_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal to a High Court from an appellate decree of a subordinate court.
predicates.substantial_question_formulated: The High Court formulated a question as a substantial question of law for the appeal.
predicates.formulated_question_not_decided: The High Court did not decide the substantial question it had formulated.
predicates.evidence_reappraised_without_additional_: The High Court reappreciated evidence without formulating an additional substantial question of law and recording reasons for doing so.
predicates.high_court_must_confine_decision_to_prop: The High Court must decide the appeal within the scope of substantial questions of law properly formulated for it.

issues.definition: When a High Court hears a second appeal in which a substantial question has been formulated, it must decide within the properly formulated questions rather than reappreciate evidence outside that scope.

issues.legal_issue: A High Court cannot disturb findings of fact in a second appeal merely by reappreciating the evidence; it may do so only where the findings are perverse.
material_facts: The courts below found that the earlier sale was sham and nominal, that a customary divorce had occurred, and that the alleged heirship had not been proved.
The High Court reappreciated the evidence and reached contrary factual findings.
The High Court did not conclude that the findings of the courts below were perverse because they rested on a misreading of evidence or no evidence.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was not entitled to reverse the findings of fact, and its judgment was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: The High Court’s jurisdiction in a second appeal under Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure is limited. Findings of fact cannot be disturbed merely on a different assessment of the evidence; intervention is permissible where the findings are perverse, including where they are based on a misreading of evidence or on no evidence. The Court applied the principles governing second appeals discussed in Santosh Hazari v. Purushottam Tiwari.

rule.if: second_appeal and lower_court_factual_findings and high_court_reversed_findings_on_reappraisal and not findings_found_perverse

predicates.second_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal to a High Court from an appellate decree of a subordinate court.
predicates.lower_court_factual_findings: The courts below made findings of fact on the evidence before them.
predicates.high_court_reversed_findings_on_reapprai: The High Court reversed those findings after reassessing the evidence.
predicates.findings_found_perverse: The High Court found that the lower courts’ findings were perverse because they rested on a misreading of evidence or on no evidence.
predicates.high_court_must_not_reverse_factual_find: The High Court must not reverse the lower courts’ factual findings on the basis of reappreciation alone.

issues.definition: When a High Court reverses factual findings in a second appeal after reassessing evidence, it may do so only if it finds those findings perverse.

issues.legal_issue: A second appeal must not be remitted for a fresh decision when no substantial question of law arises in it.
material_facts: The respondent asked the Supreme Court to remit the matter to the High Court for a fresh decision.
The respondent could not identify a substantial question of law arising in the second appeal.
The Supreme Court concluded that no substantial question of law arose.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to remit the matter, allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court’s judgment, and restored the decisions of the courts below.
issues.legal_principle: Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure makes the existence of a substantial question of law necessary for the exercise of second-appellate jurisdiction. The Court applied the principles in Santosh Hazari v. Purushottam Tiwari and concluded that no such question arose in this case.

predicates.second_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal to a High Court from an appellate decree of a subordinate court.
predicates.no_substantial_question_arises: The case does not involve a substantial question of law that can properly be decided in the second appeal.
predicates.remand_requested: A party asks that the case be sent back for a fresh decision.
predicates.court_must_not_remit_for_fresh_second_ap: The court must not remit the case for a fresh decision of the second appeal when no substantial question of law arises.

issues.definition: When no substantial question of law arises in a second appeal, a request to send the matter back for a fresh decision does not justify remittal.
